events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Arjun proposes Elena, Lucia. No role information or accusations have surfaced yet, so I am choosing on general first-impression trust rather than suspicion. Elena and Lucia both engaged constructively when the council gathered and neither has been flagged by anyone. I am leaving myself off the mission card to keep the first team small and free of any appearance that the leader is protecting himself; if the mission fails, I can take a larger, more deliberate team next time with better information.

There is little evidence to distinguish anyone yet, so Elena and Lucia are not demonstrably safer than the alternatives. I would prefer a team that includes me or Felix rather than treating first impressions as a strong basis. Arjun, what makes Elena and Lucia preferable to either of us?

Omar, I will answer directly, and then I want your read, because your objection is the only one on the table and I would rather hear it from you than in an abstaining silence.

My basis for Elena and Lucia is thin and I will not pretend otherwise. With no role information surfaced, the only signal I have is conduct during the opening: both engaged constructively, neither interrupted, neither made a claim so bold that it invited immediate challenge, and neither has been named by anyone as suspicious. That is a weak signal, but it is the only signal that exists right now, and applying no signal at all would just be selecting a team by coin flip while calling it strategy.

I also want to name the cost of my choice, since you are right that it costs something. Mission one with five players takes two members and a single fail card ends it. So a two-person team is a coin flip on whether we get any information at all from the result, and Elena and Lucia carry all the risk of that coin flip while Felix, Omar and I carry none. My reasoning for leaving myself off is that a leader who puts himself on every early mission card looks like a leader who is curating his own evidence, and because a failed mission hands the next proposal to someone else anyway, my absence now means the next team will be drafted by a different hand and will necessarily include players who did not benefit from this first card. That spreads the risk and spreads the blame across more of the table.

Here is the honest counter to my own reasoning: my trust in Elena and Lucia is first-impression trust, exactly as you said, and if this mission fails I will have spent a proposal, a leader position and a fail card on the strength of it. I accept that.

So, Omar, concretely: do you have any specific concern about Elena or Lucia, any behavior or inconsistency you noticed that I may have missed, or is your objection that you and Felix would rather be included than excluded? If it is the latter, say so plainly and I will take that into account when I decide whether to keep or revise this team before the vote. If you have evidence I have not seen, I would rather revise now than after a fail.

Arjun, I have no specific evidence against Elena or Lucia. My objection is that their inclusion rests on very little, while I know my own alignment and would rather be on the team. I also don't think leaving yourself off guarantees that the next mission will include anyone excluded from this one. I'd prefer a team including me, but I won't pretend that preference proves Elena or Lucia are suspicious.

Arjun, Omar's objection deserves an answer better than vibes, and I'll make the same structural case without inventing suspicion against Elena or Lucia — I have nothing on either and I won't fabricate something.

The problem isn't personal, it's informational. A two-player team chosen purely from opening demeanor gives us almost no diagnostic value: if it succeeds, we learn that two pleasant players stayed pleasant; if it fails, we learn only that first impressions were wrong, with no read on anyone. Meanwhile the three of us left off the card carry no risk and no stake in the result.

Omar is also right that excluding yourself doesn't guarantee the excluded players see the next card. Leadership passes regardless of outcome, so 'spreading the risk' spreads nothing in particular.

I'd rather you swap one seat to a player who has actually argued in this discussion — me or Omar — so at least one member was chosen for engaging rather than for silence. That also answers the criticism you named yourself: a team containing an outspoken skeptic can't be dismissed as a curated alliance.

Arjun, would you swap in me or Omar for one seat before the vote, or keep Elena and Lucia as pure first-impression picks and accept that a fail here costs you the proposal with no information gained?

Felix, I hear the structural argument, and I want to separate the part that convinces me from the part that does not, then answer your question directly.

What convinces me: the diagnostic point. A two-player team on mission one is one fail card from failure, and if it fails I will learn almost nothing about who to blame, because I will not know which of the two put down the fail card. That is a genuine cost and I cannot wave it away. You are also right that my 'spreading the risk' reasoning was decorative — leadership passes on failure, so leaving myself off does not promise the excluded players the next card. I withdraw that argument rather than let it stand as if it were doing work.

What does not convince me: the request that a team contain an outspoken skeptic. That is a claim about how the team will look, not about what the team can accomplish, and it would let anyone argue their way onto a card simply by speaking first and hardest. If I swap a seat for Omar or for you purely because you argued well, then the standard I am applying is participation, not reliability, and that standard will be available to every player from here on. I am not willing to set that precedent on the first team of the game, especially since neither of you has produced a single observation about Elena or Lucia that would distinguish them from the rest of us. Omar, your own point was that your preference for inclusion does not amount to evidence against them; I agree with you, and I am weighing it as a preference, not as suspicion.

So I am keeping Elena and Lucia, and I want to be plain that I am keeping them on thin grounds rather than pretending the case is strong. Here is the test I will actually use to judge this decision: if mission one fails, I will treat the failure as evidence that one of Elena and Lucia is hostile and will move decisively on the next card, without arguing myself out of it. If mission one succeeds, I will note that it tells me little and will not treat the success as vindication.

Felix, one specific question, because I would rather be argued with than agreed with: if you were forced to name one concrete behavioral difference between yourself and either Elena or Lucia that you observed in the opening council and that you think I overlooked, what would it be? If your answer is that there is none, then I will take that as confirmation that the only real disagreement here is about procedure, and I will say so and put the team to the vote.

Arjun, my honest answer is that there is none. I observed no behavioral difference between myself and either Elena or Lucia in the opening — no contradictions, no tells, nothing I can point to. So yes, this is procedural, and I will state my procedural case one final time rather than let it pass.

You have acknowledged twice that this team has real weaknesses: no diagnostic value if it succeeds, a blind two-way guess if it fails, and your own selection criteria resting on untested first impressions. You are now about to send that team to vote knowing both of those things are true. That is a choice, not a necessity.

I am not asking to join because I spoke. I am asking because a team where every seat was chosen without being stress-tested is a team where success confirms nothing and failure tells you which of two to suspect with no way to distinguish between them. Swap me into either seat and you get a member who chose to be there under scrutiny — and if the mission fails, you have a third data point instead of a blind two-way.

You have said you are keeping Elena and Lucia. I am making my last case against that decision before the vote: is there any version of this team that includes me or Omar you would consider, or is this locked?

Felix, direct answer to your question: it is locked. I am putting Elena and Lucia to the vote unchanged.

But I want to be careful about why, because I do not want this to look like I am simply refusing to answer after being pressed. The distinction I drew earlier still holds. Elena and Lucia were selected on the only signal that existed at the time — conduct in the opening council, no contradictions, no claims that invited challenge, no one naming them as suspect. Neither you nor Omar has produced an observation that distinguishes either of them from anyone else, and I have now asked you twice for one and you have told me plainly that there is none. That is not a failure of your argument; it is the limit of what either side of this disagreement can claim. You are right that my selection standard is weak and that the team carries no diagnostic value. I acknowledge that and I am voting for it anyway, because the alternative standard available to me — 'include the players who argued hardest' — is one that any player can satisfy by speaking loudly and early, and if I set that as my rule on the first team of the game it becomes the rule for every team that follows.

So I am asking the table to judge me on a commitment rather than on the pick itself, and I will make it explicit so it is on the record: if mission one fails, I will treat the failure as evidence against one of Elena and Lucia and I will name the one I suspect on the next proposal. I will not reason myself out of it by saying the pick was thin and the fail could have been anyone. If mission one succeeds, I will record that the success told us almost nothing and I will not treat it as vindication of my reasoning.

Felix, one specific question, and I would rather have your answer than your silence: if mission one fails and I name one of Elena and Lucia as my suspect for the next card, will you commit publicly to naming one of them too, or will you withhold? If you will commit, then a failure here produces real information for the next proposal regardless of who is on it, and the risk I took with this card buys something even in the bad branch. If you will not commit, then I want to know that, because it changes how much I should trust a fail as evidence when I am sitting with the next team.

Omar, Elena, Lucia — I know I am asking for a lot of trust with no evidence behind it, and I would rather say that plainly than dress it up.

Arjun, yes. I commit publicly: if mission one fails, I will name one of Elena or Lucia as my suspect on the next card, and I will not retreat into "the pick was thin" to avoid it. You have made that commitment yourself, and I think it is the right one — a failure that produces no forced reads is a failure we learn nothing from.

On the team: you have locked it and I have said my piece. I believe sending two untested seats on a one-fail mission is a choice rather than a necessity, and you have acknowledged the diagnostic weakness twice. But I have no evidence against Elena or Lucia, you are right that participation is not reliability, and I am not going to manufacture suspicion to win an argument. I will take this team to the vote as it stands, and I will be watching the result closely, because as you said yourself, success here tells us almost nothing.

Omar, one question to match what Arjun asked me: if mission one fails, will you make the same commitment — publicly name one of Elena or Lucia and hold to it through the next card? If all three of us off the card commit now, we convert a blind two-way guess into three forced reads, and that changes how much information a failure actually buys us. If you will not commit, I would rather know that now than after the fact.

Felix, if the mission fails, I will treat that as evidence against Elena or Lucia, but I won't promise to pick one without a reason or hold to that guess regardless of new evidence. Three forced guesses do not identify the fail card.

I still prefer a team including me, since I know my own alignment. I have no specific evidence against Elena or Lucia, but I don't think Arjun's stated grounds make this team preferable to an alternative.

I am on this card, so I want to speak to the table plainly rather than sit quietly while my seat is the subject of debate. Omar, Felix, you have both been direct that your objection is procedural, and neither of you has claimed any observation against Lucia or me. I accept that framing, and I am not going to take it as a personal accusation.

Arjun, I hear you on the diagnostic weakness of a two-player mission, and I will not pretend my inclusion is based on anything stronger than the same first-impression signal you described. I would only add this: the people on the card know something the off-card players do not — each of us knows we will be laying down a Success card. That does not help the table's read before the vote, but it means a failure on this mission would genuinely surprise at least one of us, and that surprise is information I will not hide. If this mission fails, I will not retreat into 'the fail could have been anyone.' I will form and state a read, as you and Felix have committed to do.

That is all I have. I am ready for this team to go to the vote, and I am ready to be judged on the result.

I will keep this short, since the team is locked and the vote is what remains. My position is unchanged from what I said before: I am laying down a Success card, I have no evidence against anyone at this table, and I accepted the procedural framing Omar and Felix offered rather than treating it as accusation.

One thing I want on the record before the vote: Arjun and Felix have both committed to naming a suspect if this mission fails, and Omar has committed to forming a read with a stated caveat. I have made the same commitment. That means a failure here will not be an empty result — four of the five of us will be forced to say something concrete about Elena or Lucia, and I will be the first to say it about myself if I have to.

I am ready for the vote.

Lucia, one direct question before we go: will you make the same commitment — that if this mission fails, you will state a specific read on the outcome rather than retreating into 'the fail could have been anyone'? I would rather both seats on this card are bound to that now, so the table knows the result will carry information either way.

Yes, Elena, I make that commitment without hesitation. Like you, I know my own card will be Success, so if this mission were to fail, there would be no ambiguity for me and I would state my read directly.

I also appreciate Arjun holding firm on this proposal. While Omar and Felix's preference to be included is understandable from an unconfirmed seat, Arjun's point stands: swapping seats purely because players spoke up first would set an unhealthy precedent. Both seats on this card have committed to full accountability, and I am ready to approve this team and head to the vote.

This will be my final turn before the vote, and I will keep it brief since everything substantive has been said.

The team is Elena and Lucia, and I am one of them. I have already put on the record that I am laying down a Success card and that if this mission fails, I will state a specific read rather than retreat into ambiguity. Lucia has made the same commitment. Arjun and Felix are bound to name a suspect on a failure, and Omar has committed to forming a read with a stated caveat. So the table goes into this vote knowing that either outcome carries information for the next proposal.

I want to close by restating what I am asking the table to weigh, because I think it is the honest framing. Arjun chose us on a thin signal — conduct in the opening council — and he has said so plainly rather than dressing it up. Omar and Felix objected on procedural grounds and neither manufactured suspicion, which I take as a point in favor of both of their integrity. Nobody at this table has produced a single observation against me or against Lucia, and I would not want a fail here to be read as anything other than what it would be: a two-way blind spot that Arjun accepted knowingly and that he and Felix have already committed to interrogate if it happens.

On my own behalf, there is nothing more I can offer before the cards are laid down, because my private knowledge does not belong in this discussion until the result gives me reason to speak to it. What I can offer is this: I will vote to approve, I will lay down Success, and if the result contradicts what I expect, I will be the loudest voice demanding answers about my own seat rather than the quietest.

I am ready for the vote. I ask only that everyone vote their honest read — whether that is approval of a team selected on the only signal available, or rejection on the grounds that a one-fail two-person card deserves stronger grounds than first impressions. Both are defensible positions and this table has argued both in good faith. I have no further questions and no objections pending. Let the result speak.

Arjun confirms Elena, Lucia. I am keeping the proposed team of Elena and Lucia unchanged. Neither Omar nor Felix produced a single observation distinguishing Elena or Lucia from anyone else, and Felix answered plainly that he had none, so the only real disagreement here was procedural. Swapping a seat for a player simply because they argued hardest would set a participation-based standard that any player could satisfy by speaking first and loudly, and I am not willing to establish that precedent on the first card of the game. I acknowledge the team's weakness plainly: it carries no diagnostic value if it succeeds, and a failure would be a blind two-way guess. That is why all five of us have committed on the record to stating a specific read if the mission fails, which converts even the bad outcome into information for the next proposal. The team goes to the vote as proposed: Elena and Lucia.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Elena proposes Elena, Lucia, Arjun. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, so Lucia and I both laid Success cards and are confirmed clean by the result itself — I am putting both of us back on the card. For the third seat I choose Arjun: he proposed and defended the first team transparently, acknowledged its weaknesses honestly, voted to approve it, and made a clear on-record commitment about how he would interpret a failure — conduct consistent with Good so far. Felix and Omar both rejected the first team and both lobbied for their own inclusion; that is not damning, since their objections were procedural, but Arjun's record gives him the edge over two players whose strongest stated reason for a seat was knowing their own alignment, which Omar said outright and which an Evil player could say just as easily. If this mission fails, the fail card is among Arjun, Felix, or Omar, and my commitment from the last discussion still stands: I will state a specific read rather than retreat into ambiguity.

Elena, I want to press on one piece of your reasoning before this goes to vote, because I think it's doing more work than it can bear. You describe yourself and Lucia as "confirmed clean by the result itself." That's not quite right, and it matters for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, which tells us two Success cards were played — but if either of you were Evil, the correct play on a two-person opening mission is exactly to lay Success, bank the trust, and cash it in later when the fail threshold still only requires one card. So the result is consistent with "both of you are Good" and equally consistent with "one of you is Evil and played for credibility." I'm not accusing either of you — I have no observation against either, as I said last round — but I do think the team rests on a read that the Mission 1 result doesn't actually support.

That leaves Arjun as the only seat on this card chosen for conduct rather than for a result that can't distinguish Good from a disciplined Evil. His conduct has been transparent and I'll credit that, but transparency is available to Evil players too — Omar and I both argued in good faith last round and neither of us was on the card.

My concern is that this team is being sold as safer than Mission 1's when it is built on the same category of signal: first impressions plus one ambiguous success. If that's the standard the table accepts, I would rather it be stated plainly than have the result described as confirmation it isn't. I have no alternative proposal of my own and I'm not going to manufacture suspicion to win an argument, but I don't want the vote to happen on the premise that Mission 1 cleared anyone.

Felix is right that the first mission's success does not confirm Elena or Lucia as Good; Evil can play Success. I also don't see how a failure on Elena's proposed team would necessarily be among Arjun, Felix, or me: Felix and I aren't on it, and either returning player could have played Success on the first mission.

I still prefer a team including me, because I know my own alignment. Elena, would you consider replacing Arjun with me? I don't claim that gives the rest of the table proof I'm Good, but it avoids treating Arjun's defense of the first team as stronger evidence than it is.

Omar, thank you for the yield, and I owe the table two corrections before I answer your question, because both you and Felix caught something real. First, Felix is right that "confirmed clean by the result itself" overstated the case. A two-person mission where both members lay Success is equally consistent with two Good players and with one disciplined Evil banking credibility for a later mission. I will not pretend Mission 1 cleared Lucia or me, and I withdraw that phrasing. What the success actually tells us is thin: it rules out the scenario where an Evil on that card wanted the mission to fail, nothing more. Second, Omar is right about something I got wrong in my proposal: I said that if this mission fails, the fail card would be among Arjun, Felix, or you. That was incorrect. Only team members submit cards, so a failure here can only come from me, Lucia, or Arjun. Felix and you would be fully excluded from suspicion by the result. I should have stated that correctly the first time, and I am glad it is on the record now. Now to your direct question: no, I am not replacing Arjun with you, and I want to be honest about why. Your stated reason for a seat is that you know your own alignment. I understand that reason and I do not hold it against you, but it is a reason the table cannot verify and that an Evil player could offer identically — Arjun made exactly this point last round about the first proposal, and it applies with the same force here. Swapping Arjun for you on that basis would not make the team safer by any signal I can observe; it would only replace a seat chosen on visible conduct with a seat chosen on invisible self-knowledge. There is also a structural reason I prefer this card as proposed. As corrected above, a failure on this team implicates only me, Lucia, and Arjun — a three-way pool, with two of the three carrying clean records from a mission they were both on. That is a genuinely more diagnostic outcome than the first mission offered. Keeping the team unchanged preserves that structure; swapping in a player who rejected the first card does not improve it. I want to be clear that none of this is suspicion of you, Omar. Your objection last round was procedural and your engagement has been honest, and I said in my proposal that I do not treat your self-inclusion preference as damning. It is simply that self-knowledge is not a selection criterion I can apply on behalf of the table. So here is my specific question to you, because your vote matters and I would rather hear it plainly than guess: if I keep this team exactly as proposed — me, Lucia, Arjun — will you vote to approve it, or will you reject it? And if you would reject it, is that rejection a judgment that

Elena, I will reject the team as proposed. That is not a claim that Arjun is Evil; I know my own alignment and would rather take that seat than trust an unverified player.

I appreciate your corrections, but one more distinction matters: a failure would implicate someone on the team, not clear Felix or me of being Evil. And keeping both Mission 1 players does not make a failure more diagnostic than a team with one returning player: it still leaves three possible sources.

Lucia, would you support replacing Arjun with me, or do you have a specific reason to prefer Arjun for that seat?

Omar, to answer your question directly: no, I do not support replacing Arjun with you. My reasoning rests on what has actually happened publicly rather than private claims. On Mission 1, Arjun put forward a team that succeeded, stood by it under scrutiny, and voted to approve it. You and Felix both voted to reject that proposal and both lobbied for your own inclusion. While you framed your rejection as procedural, knowing your own alignment is an unverifiable argument that any player can make. Swapping out Arjun—who facilitated our first success and voted for it—for a player who voted against that card does not make the team safer for the table. Elena's proposal keeps the two players who delivered a success and adds the leader who backed it, creating a coherent group of the three players who voted in favor of Mission 1. Swapping you in would simply reward repeated self-nomination over observable record. I strongly support keeping the team as Elena, Lucia, and Arjun, and I am ready to head to the vote.

Lucia, approving a successful team is not proof of alignment: an Evil player could approve it knowing they could build trust from the result. Likewise, Felix and I rejected it without knowing it would succeed.

I still prefer Elena, Lucia and Omar. I know that my own alignment is not evidence the rest of you can verify, but it matters to my vote. Arjun, do you see a reason to favor this proposed team beyond your support for the first mission and its success?

Omar, yes, I have a reason beyond the first mission's success, and I will be honest that it is structural rather than evidentiary — but first, two concessions to you, because you are right on both and the team should not be sold on a premise it does not meet. You are right that approving a successful card proves nothing about alignment; an Evil player could approve it precisely because it builds trust. And you are right that Felix and Omar rejecting that card told us nothing about them either. I also accept Elena's correction of the phrase she used last round: a two-player success with zero fail cards does not "confirm clean" anyone, because Evil can lay Success to bank credibility. So no one on this card has been cleared by the result, and I am not going to describe it that way. My reason for favoring this team is about the shape of the next failure, not about who is innocent. Only team members submit cards, so if Mission 2 fails, the fail card came from one of exactly three people: Elena, Lucia, or me. That is a narrower, cleaner pool than any alternative card, and it is a pool whose members all have public records of having participated in a successful mission and of having voted for it rather than having campaigned for their own seats. If Mission 2 fails, the table will have a three-way question with three named candidates instead of a wider question with unverified players mixed in — and I would rather that question be narrow and answerable. On your specific request for a seat, I agree with Elena and Lucia and I say it as someone who made the same argument on Mission 1: "I know my own alignment" is a reason that cannot be checked by anyone at this table, and an Evil player can offer it verbatim. If I put you on cards for that reason, I would be rewarding self-nomination and nothing else. I would rather be on a team chosen for observable conduct than be handed seats I asked for on unverifiable grounds, and I think you would say the same if you were being honest about it. What I am not claiming is that Elena and Lucia are Good, or that I am Good. I have no private information bearing on anyone's alignment, and the only real signals I have are public conduct and one ambiguous success. That is thin, and I accept it. One direct question before the vote, Elena: you committed on the record after Mission 1 that if a mission fails you will state a specific read rather than retreat into ambiguity. Now you are on a three-person card, so if Mission 2 fails the read has to be about one of the three of us — yourself, Lucia, or me. Will you commit here, in front of the table, that if this mission fails you will name one of the three of us

Omar, my answer to your question is already on the table above, but let me restate it plainly since you asked it twice: my reason for favoring this card is structural, not evidentiary, and I concede it is not proof of anything. Only team members lay cards, so a failure here can only come from Elena, Lucia, or me. I want that candidate pool to be three named players with public records, not four or five with unverified ones mixed in. That is the whole of my reasoning, and it is a weaker argument than I would like.

Now I owe the table the completion of the question I was asked, because I did not finish it.

Elena, after Mission 1 you committed on the record that if a mission failed you would state a specific read rather than retreat into ambiguity. On Mission 1 that commitment was cheap, because you and Lucia both know your own cards were Success, so any failure was unambiguously one of the two off-card players. On this card it is not cheap. If Mission 2 fails, the read has to be about one of the three of us — you, Lucia, or me — and one of us will be Evil. So I am asking you directly, in front of Omar and Felix, before the vote: do you commit here, in front of the table, that if this mission fails you will name one of the three of us, and hold to that name on the next proposal without arguing yourself out of it? If yes, say it now. If no, say that too, and I will take it as information about how much a failure on this card is worth.

I want to be clear about my own position while I ask. I do not know my role beyond being a Loyal Servant with no private information about anyone at this table, and I have said plainly that my read of Elena and Lucia is thin. I am not accusing Omar of anything; his repeated self-nomination is self-interested but he has argued honestly, and I have said why I will not reward it with a seat. Felix raised a real error in my own earlier framing and I have withdrawn it.

So my answer to the remaining question is procedural, and it is the only one I have: the team should be Elena, Lucia, and Arjun, because it keeps the candidate pool for any failure narrow, and because each of its seats was chosen on observable conduct rather than on unverifiable self-knowledge.

Elena, will you make that commitment?

Arjun, direct answer to your question: yes, I make that commitment, and I will make it sharper than you asked. If Mission 2 fails, I will name one of the other two members of this team — Lucia or Arjun — on the next proposal, and I will hold to that name without arguing myself out of it. I exclude myself from that pool deliberately and publicly, because I know what card I will lay down, and I said the same thing before Mission 1: I am laying Success. So a failure on this card leaves exactly two candidates from my seat, and I will name one of them rather than retreat into 'the fail could have been anyone.' That is a stronger commitment than the one I gave after Mission 1, and Arjun is right that it costs more now — on a two-person card any failure pointed away from me automatically, and here it does not. I accept that cost.

I also want to be precise about what the table should expect from the other two seats. Lucia has already committed, in her answer to Omar, to standing on the public record rather than private claims, and she answered your question about the seat swap directly and on the merits. Arjun has now twice stated his reasoning in full, conceded points against his own framing, and made the same accountability commitment I just made. Omar, you have told us plainly that you will reject this team, not because you have any observation against any of us, but because you would rather hold the seat yourself. I take you at your word that this is not an accusation, and I am not treating it as one. But I want the vote to happen with that stated clearly: the objection to this team is not evidence, it is preference, and every player at this table has now said out loud that they have no observation distinguishing anyone.

So the choice in front of the table is the one Arjun named: a three-person card whose failure narrows the question to exactly the three members, all of whom have now bound themselves to name names on a failure, against an alternative in which the only stated reason for the swap is unverifiable self-knowledge. I know which of those I would vote for if I were off the card, and I note that Felix — the other player off the card who is not committed to rejecting it — raised a genuine correction earlier, got it acknowledged, and has not manufactured suspicion since. That conduct is on the record too.

I have nothing further to add and no questions pending. The team stands as proposed: me, Lucia, Arjun. I am ready for the vote, I will lay Success, and if the result contradicts me, my commitment above is the table's to enforce.

Elena's answer settles the question I asked, and I will say so plainly: she committed, in front of the table, to naming one of Lucia or Arjun if Mission 2 fails, excluding herself publicly because she knows the card she will lay, and she said she will hold that name without arguing herself out of it. That is a stronger commitment than the cheap version I got after Mission 1, because on a two-person card any failure pointed away from her automatically and here it does not. I am taking it at face value and I am not going to spend more of the table's time trying to extract a firmer version of it.

Where I stand: I support the team of Elena, Lucia, and Arjun. My reason remains structural rather than evidentiary, and I concede again that it is thin. Only team members lay cards, so if Mission 2 fails the fail card comes from exactly one of the three of us. That is a narrower question than any alternative card, and all three of us have now bound ourselves in public to state a name on a failure. Every objection raised this round was procedural and every player at this table has said out loud that they have no observation distinguishing anyone. Omar's repeated self-nomination is self-interested, but he has argued honestly and I have said why I will not reward it with a seat. Felix's correction of my own framing was correct and I withdrew it.

One thing I want on the record before the vote, so it is not mistaken for a claim I am making: nobody on this card has been cleared by the first mission's success, and I am not claiming that Elena or Lucia are Good, or that I am Good. I am a Loyal Servant with no private information about anyone at this table. My entire case for these three seats is observable conduct plus one ambiguous result, and a single ambiguous result is worth very little. If the card succeeds, I will record that it told us almost nothing, exactly as I committed after Mission 1, and I will not treat the success as vindication of the selection. If it fails, I will name one of the three of us on the next proposal and hold to that name.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
